view: Ḍuḥā can mean the whole daylight or day, set against night. Support includes Arabic usage for appearing in sunlight and Qurʾānic contrasts of night with punishment arriving at ḍuḥā.
note: Alūsī reports an objection based on the following dark night, then rejects the assumption that the night must be intensely dark. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ argues against this whole-day sense.

view: Ḍuḥā denotes a bounded morning period: the early part of day or forenoon as the sun rises, spreads light, and climbs higher; some descriptions specify its temperate late-morning hour.
note: Descriptions range from the day's first hour to the interval after sunrise when the sun is high; al-Ālūsī prefers the interval over sunlight or the rising itself.

view: A narrower gloss identifies ḍuḥā with sunrise itself, rather than a span of morning.
Ḍuḥā can refer to the visible sun's light or morning brightness; its root evokes visibility and exposure to sunlight, and some uses extend to what occurs then or what sunlight makes visible.
Qurʾānic use of ḍuḥā opposite evening, for the sun's light, and as an appointed hour supports a specific daytime period; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ argues these examples weigh against the whole-day reading.
note: Her cited passages include 79:29, 79:46, 7:98, 20:59, and 91:1.

view: The sacrificial day is called aḍḥā after the sheep sacrificed at ḍuḥā.
Ḍuḥā has also been glossed as the forenoon prayer.
The word's sense is treated elsewhere in the commentaries on the sun and its ḍuḥā in 91:1.
The morning time is named by metonymy, or an omitted noun such as 'time' is understood to make its reference parallel to night.
The definite article may mark ḍuḥā generically, but Elmalılı prefers a specific dawn of truth: the Muhammadan mission beginning to radiate mercy and light.
The final alif is written with an alif shape because the form comes from ḍaḥā yaḍḥū.
note: Competing orthographic accounts appear in the following views.

view: Spelling should record pronunciation, not the supposed yāʾ or wāw origin of a root; root-based spellings conflict with spoken forms, conventional and Qurʾānic spellings, and examples such as rāmā, ghazā, mā zakkā, rabayān, and yarbū.
note: Al-Naḥḥās rejects the Kufan convention; the examples and the objection about the dual are transmitted from other grammarians.

view: ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān relays an allegation that al-Akhfash and al-Kisāʾī devised the root-based spelling convention for profit and influence and that al-Kisāʾī's political position spread it.
The muṣḥaf writes the final alif of al-ḍuḥā in a yāʾ shape despite its wāw root, matching other endings, most of them yāʾ-rooted, and supporting imāla in relevant dialects.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Ibn Mālik on the spelling pattern.

view: At this word the reading difference concerns imāla versus open or emphatic pronunciation, while the phrase remains an oath.

Readers differ in imāla of these endings: Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir use open forms; al-Kisāʾī inclines all; Ḥamza distinguishes yāʾ and wāw origins; Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr have transmitted intermediate, open, or inclined forms with differing scope.
note: Abū ʿAmr is also described as following the sūrah's ending pattern; Medinans use a middle degree in one account.

view: Imāla is ordinarily licensed when an alif behaves like one originating in yāʾ, including derived verbs and nouns; wāw-origin alifs usually resist it, and rare exceptions do not overturn that rule.
Verbs of wāw origin can nevertheless be inclined when their inflected forms shift to yāʾ, as with ḍuḥā and sajā.
The wording is an oath by ḍuḥā or its light.
An implied 'Lord' is the oath's object: the sense is 'by the Lord of morning' and likewise of night.
note: This differs from taking the created time itself as the oath object.

view: The oath can single out the morning when God spoke to Moses and the magicians prostrated or people assembled; the hour's honor recalls divine speech and suggests that God can honor Muhammad and turn enemies' hearts.
note: Some name Moses' speech alone or the prostration alone. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects the linkage as anachronistic because the cited passages were revealed later.

view: One interpretation pairs the morning of Moses' divine speech with the night of the Prophet's Night Journey or Ascension.
The forenoon is singled out as the day's youthful, vigorous, bright, and honored phase, fitting the Prophet's exceptional rank.
Midmorning brings people together and ease after night's isolation, so its oath promises renewed revelation and comfort after the Prophet's distress during the pause.
Morning brightness represents revelation's light spreading through the world like sunrise.
The oath by morning light draws attention to a great sign and blessing among created things, and created things in oaths can be glorified as signs.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ treats glorification as a possible impression rather than the device's central function.

view: The oath's wāw strongly directs attention to familiar sensory realities that prepare the reader for unseen meanings; the quality chosen for the oath suits its context.
note: This is Bint al-Shāṭiʾ's preferred account of its rhetorical function.

view: Although ḍuḥā admits several lexical senses, the setting's rhetoric selects a single fitting sense here.

The order of this morning oath before night gives daylight priority through its intrinsic and incidental honor; night leads in the preceding sūrah because darkness is the original state to which air returns after sunset.
A short hour of ḍuḥā balances a whole night as Muhammad balances all prophets and their communities; brief joy similarly balances longer worldly sorrow and anxiety.
A reported parable has a black cloud rain grief for three hundred years and a white cloud rain joy for one hour, explaining prolonged common sorrow and rare brief joy.
Some explain the order of morning then night as preferring life until believers mature, avoiding despair first and fear of divine plotting later.
Bint al-Shāṭiʾ finds no clear link between the oath and its answer in al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, and Abū Ḥayyān, and says they neglect comparison with explicit Qurʾānic denials of oaths.

The daily sequence of bright morning and quiet night pictures revelation's pause and return as part of wise change, without implying that heaven abandoned earth; light and darkness can also picture guidance and truth against misguidance and falsehood.
Morning as first revelation gives life and activity; night as quiet rest restores strength for later work, and renewed revelation relieves the Prophet's distress.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ objects that this explanation nearly loses the sensory analogy.

view: The bright morning after darkness and revelation after its pause are presented as proof of God's lordship, wisdom, and mercy.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ objects that doubt about lordship misses the occasion's claim of abandonment.

view: The oath answers the unbelievers' taunt because they could not prove that God had abandoned Muhammad.
Night and day alternately prevail; created people likewise undergo change and are not exempt from it.
Light and dark alternation displays the Creator's power.
The oath's paired morning and night create a tender, reflective setting, making the spirit sense creation worshipping its Maker and the Prophet feel accompanied in a living universe.
The sūrah's graceful diction and musical cadence embody its gentleness and point to God's unmatched creative work.
Morning is bright youthful joy and revealed knowledge, while settled night provides rest before renewal; the pairing introduces reassurance that the Prophet has not been abandoned.
Day and night together are divine mercy: night permits rest, and day renewed work and pursuit of bounty; both sustain the world.
Morning brightness evokes revelation and guidance; settled night evokes the Prophet's audible Qurʾān recitation and perhaps his night prayer.

The opening oath rebuts idolaters who inferred a halt in revelation from several nights when the Prophet did not recite; the warning addresses their insinuation, while the Prophet himself had no doubt.
The morning brightness inwardly represents the spirit.
Dawn is God's unveiling of the inner secret while the servant calls people through attention to creation.
Ḍuḥā is the station of witnessing, while settled night is the inner eye's veil or ghayn clouding the heart, as evoked by a Prophetic report.
Day and night signify disclosure and veiling, divine gentleness and severity, and the lights of beauty and traces of majesty.
Morning can symbolize the Prophet's bright face and night his dark hair.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects this and related esoteric readings.

view: Other symbolic readings pair morning and night as the Garden's light and the Fire's darkness, or enlightened knowers' hearts and disbelievers' blackened hearts.
Esoteric readings also make morning and night male and female relatives, knowledge and forgiveness, or Islam's rise and later estrangement.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects these readings.

view: The sūrah title's daylight symbolizes the spiritual light of perfected character and divine favor in both lives.
Mixed and pure light and darkness symbolize clear and ambiguous Qurʾānic teachings and changing human spiritual states.
The heart's light can overcome the soul's darkness, while appetite can darken a person; spirit or temperament then elevates or degrades them.
Opening night evokes uncertainty about one's path and destiny; divine signs and refuge bring certainty, as obscurity gives way to the clarity of hearts strengthened by God.
The Prophet's illness or absence from night prayer for one to three nights prompted a woman's taunt that his satan had left him; the opening verses were revealed in response.
note: Reports vary between one or two and two or three nights; some expressly mention illness.

view: A stone injured the Prophet's finger; after he stopped rising for two or three nights, a woman said his devil had left, and the verses were revealed.
note: Ibn Kathīr calls the injury report authentic but its causal link unusual; al-Tirmidhī authenticated a version.

view: After a pause in Gabriel's visits or revelation, polytheists claimed that God had abandoned or hated Muhammad; the opening verses answered the claim.
The taunting woman is identified as Umm Jamīl, Abū Lahab's wife; one report places her confrontation after the sūrah about Abū Lahab.
One Jundub report identifies the taunter as a cousin's daughter, who said the Prophet's companion had left him when Gabriel was withheld.
Khadīja, concerned by the Prophet's distress during delayed revelation, said she feared his Lord had rejected him; then the sūrah came.
note: Ibn Ḥajar distinguishes her compassionate concern from Umm Jamīl's spite. Some transmissions are mursal.

view: A proposed occasion says Jews asked about Dhū al-Qarnayn, the Cave Companions, and the Spirit; the Prophet promised an answer next day without saying 'if God wills,' and revelation paused.
A puppy in the Prophet's house delayed Gabriel, because angels do not enter a house with a dog or image.
In a fuller puppy account, a dead puppy hidden beneath the Prophet's bed held up revelation for four days; Khawla found it, Gabriel returned, and verses through 'you will be satisfied' descended.
note: Ibn Ḥajar rejects this as the specific occasion because it conflicts with sound reports, while accepting that a puppy once delayed Gabriel.

view: A reported explanation for the pause blames failure to clean between fingers and trim nails; the Prophet says revelation could not descend amid that neglect.
Reported durations of revelation's pause differ: twelve, fifteen, twenty-five, forty, or fifty days or mornings.
note: Ibn Jurayj gives twelve, Ibn ʿAbbās fifteen, Muqātil forty; forty mornings, twenty-five days, and fifty days also appear.

view: On Gabriel's return with the sūrah, the Prophet said he missed him; Gabriel replied he had longed for the Prophet too but could descend only by God's command.
note: The explanation invokes 19:64, that angels descend only by their Lord's command.

view: One account links Gabriel's delayed greeting, the Prophet's joy, and his takbīr with the revelation of al-Ḍuḥā after Quraysh claimed that God had abandoned him.
note: This version puts the pause at forty mornings.

view: Revelation and Gabriel's visits sustained the Prophet amid rejection and persecution; their interruption left him isolated and distressed.
The sūrah comforts the Prophet with assurance that God has not abandoned him, promises future satisfaction, recalls earlier care, and calls for care of the vulnerable and preaching.
note: Quṭb emphasizes hope, closeness, calm, and the afterlife's superiority.

view: The later reminder of God's past care supports al-Ḍuḥā's reassurance that the One who first blessed the Prophet will continue doing so.
The preceding sūrah ends by promising satisfaction to the most pious; al-Ḍuḥā turns to the Prophet and God's gifts and honors for him.

One explanation links the preceding sūrah to Abū Bakr and this one to the Messenger, with no sūrah between them to suggest closeness, while denying that Abū Bakr's preceding position proves superiority.
note: The argument compares an oath by creation preceding an oath by God.

view: Al-Ālūsī rejects the Imam's flower metaphor for the relation of this sūrah to the previous one as untenable.
Sūrahs 93 and 94 form a pair promising success: the former reflects intense Meccan opposition and external needs, while the latter shows emerging success and spiritual relief.
The discourse moves from day and night as models of developmental trials to reassurance, better times, past divine help, and duties arising from those favors.
Al-Ḍuḥā is Meccan.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says its Meccan status is undisputed; Study Quran calls it early Meccan.

view: The sūrah is counted as ten verses in one account and eleven, unanimously in another.
note: The counts disagree.

view: Proposed revelation orders differ: after 'Read' and al-Muddaththir came al-Qalam through 'great character,' then al-Ḍuḥā; another placement puts it eleventh after al-Fajr; other rankings give fourth or seventh.
Al-Ḍuḥā may have been the first sūrah revealed whole; another account gives that place to al-Fātiḥah.
Some say Sūrahs 93 and 94 were originally one because Companions recited them in a single prayer cycle without a separating basmala.
A transmitted practice begins takbīr at al-Ḍuḥā and continues through the Qurʾān's end, saying 'Allāhu akbar' and, in one account, the basmala at each sūrah's ending.
note: One transmission is attributed to Ibn Kathīr; another gives a Prophetic instruction.

view: A reported virtue promises intercession and reward for reciting Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā, scaled to every orphan and petitioner.
The Prophet reportedly instructed worshippers to use the Sun and Midmorning sūrahs in the two ḍuḥā prayer units.
The ḍuḥā prayer is unanimously a sunnah; its time runs from when the sun is high until shortly before noon.
Abū Ḥanīfa sets the ḍuḥā prayer at two or four units with one salutation; Mālik sets no fixed upper limit; al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad require at least two, with maxima of twelve and eight respectively.
note: Most Shāfiʿī authorities adopt eight as the maximum, which al-Nawawī validates.

view: A sound report says the Prophet prayed eight ḍuḥā units in Umm Hānī's house during the conquest of Mecca, and had prayed ḍuḥā earlier too.
A noncanonical reading of the later 'mā waddaʿaka' lightens its consonant, against the standard doubled form.
note: Attributed to the Prophet and ʿUrwa.

view: The light verb wadaʿ in the later verse is rare; Arabic normally uses taraka instead, illustrated with Abū al-Aswad's poetry.
The later sajā means night becoming still and calm, illustrated by poetry about a tranquil sea and quiet night.
Reports gloss the following night as arriving, settling, departing, or becoming still and quiet among its people.
note: These are competing senses of sajā in verse 2.
